uncited: Spatial Indexing and Ordering provides the mechanisms to map multi-dimensional voxel coordinates to linear memory indices and to organize data in memory to maximize spatial locality for cache-coherent access.

It solves the problem of inefficient memory access patterns in volume rendering by ensuring that spatially adjacent voxels are stored in adjacent memory locations, thereby reducing cache misses during ray marching and data loading.

It sets itself apart from hierarchical indexing methods (like [Morton Code Generation for Octrees](4673-morton-code-generation-for-octrees.md)) by focusing on flat linearization and sorting strategies rather than tree-based culling, and from pure storage formats by defining the algorithmic mapping between logical space and physical memory.
All methods in this family share the goal of preserving spatial locality in linear memory.
The core mechanism involves transforming $N$-dimensional coordinates $(x, y, z)$ into a 1D index $I$ such that points close in Euclidean distance have close indices $I$.
**Linearization:** Mapping 3D grid coordinates to a 1D array using arithmetic strides (row-major) or bit-interleaving (Morton/Z-order).
**Locality Preservation:** Ensuring that the mapping function minimizes the distance between indices of spatially neighboring voxels.
**Coordinate Transformation:** Converting world-space ray positions into grid-local indices using transformation matrices or scaling factors.
For space-filling curves, the mapping is non-linear but preserves locality better than simple strides.
The concept of linearizing multi-dimensional data for cache efficiency is fundamental to computer graphics.
Morton codes (Z-order) were introduced by G. M. Morton in 1966 [S7, unofficial].
